GDPR Art. 17 requires erasure 'without undue delay' when one of the listed grounds applies. Art. 12(3) sets the outer limit for acting on a request: one month from receipt, extendable by two further months for complex or numerous requests if the person is told why within the first month. Erasure is also not unconditional: Art. 17(3) exempts data needed for legal obligations, public-interest tasks, archiving or research, and for establishing or defending legal claims. 'Hard delete everything within one month' is a fair one-line version, but it leaves out both the extension and the exceptions.
precise_version: On a valid erasure request the controller must erase the data without undue delay, and must act on the request within one month (extendable by two more months), unless an Art. 17(3) exception such as legal claims applies.

note: GDPR does allow time: one month, extendable by two further months, so up to three in total, not 'one to two'. But the extension is for complex or numerous requests, and the base duty is 'without undue delay'; the window is not breathing space for keeping data in case of harassment. Keeping data because it may be needed for a legal claim (for example a harassment complaint) is handled by the separate Art. 17(3)(e) exception, which applies regardless of the deadline.
precise_version: GDPR gives one month to act on an erasure request, extendable by two months for complex cases; data needed for legal claims can be kept under a specific exception, not by using the deadline.

note: Describes a common practice, but as a compliance claim it misleads. Logs that contain a user's personal data are personal data. When a valid erasure request has no exemption, the ICO says erasure covers backup systems as well as live systems. Copies that cannot be erased at once must be put 'beyond use' until they are overwritten. Keeping logs so data can be 'recovered' after an erasure request is not a GDPR-compliant hack.
precise_version: Live PII can be deleted at once; copies in logs and backups must be kept beyond use and overwritten on their normal schedule, not kept so the data can be recovered.

note: The Atlassian outage happened: on 5 April 2022 a script deleted 883 sites for 775 customers, and restoration took up to 14 days (all restored by 18 April). But it was an operational mistake, not a GDPR erasure. A deletion script was given site IDs instead of app IDs, and Atlassian restored the sites from its 30-day full and incremental backups. Recovering accidentally deleted data from backups is what backups are for. It does not show that companies ignore erasure requests, and GDPR guidance accepts backup copies that are kept beyond use and overwritten on schedule.

Largely matches regulator guidance. The ICO accepts that backup copies may not be erasable at once, provided they are put 'beyond use' (not restored or used for any other purpose) and overwritten on the normal retention schedule. The individual must also be told what will happen to their data in backups. 'The data remains there' is fine only under those conditions.
precise_version: Historical snapshots are usually not rewritten, but the erased user's data in them must be kept beyond use and must age out on the backup retention schedule.

note: Calling these 'hacks' to 'maximize what you can' suggests ways around the law. The practices that are legitimate (backups kept beyond use, data kept under an Art. 17(3) exception) are recognised parts of the rules, documented in regulator guidance, not loopholes.

GDPR does not apply to every organization everywhere. Under Art. 3 it covers organizations established in the EU, and organizations outside the EU that offer goods or services to people in the EU or monitor their behaviour there. Within scope, erasure is a right only on the grounds listed in Art. 17(1) (for example, consent withdrawn or data no longer needed), and Art. 17(3) exceptions apply. Other laws (UK GDPR, CCPA/CPRA) grant similar rights with different rules.
precise_version: GDPR applies to organizations in the EU or serving or monitoring people in the EU; within that scope users can demand erasure on specified grounds, subject to exceptions.

True for values in the common case: Redis and Memcached store the bytes the client sends, and compressing them is the client's job (client libraries such as pymemcache offer opt-in zlib compression above a size threshold). Redis does compress internally in two narrow places: LZF compression of strings in RDB snapshot files (on by default), and optional LZF compression of inner list nodes (list-compress-depth, off by default).

The teacher was unsure; here is the answer. The usual place for cache compression is the client library, not a server plugin. For example, pymemcache's CompressedSerde compresses values above 400 bytes with zlib by default and keeps the original bytes if compression does not shrink them. Redis itself compresses only RDB snapshot files and, optionally, list internals.
precise_version: Cache compression is usually done by the client library (for example pymemcache's CompressedSerde), not by the cache server.

note: Correct as stated: compression has per-value overhead, so tiny values gain nothing; pymemcache, for example, only compresses values longer than 400 bytes and keeps the original if compression doesn't shrink it.

CDNs do compress text responses (Cloudflare applies Gzip, Brotli or Zstandard to HTML, CSS, JS, JSON and similar). Images, audio and video are already compressed by their formats, though, and MDN advises against compressing them again because the overhead can make files larger. For media, savings come from format and resolution choices (for example modern image codecs, adaptive bitrate video), not from generic compression.
precise_version: CDNs compress text responses; images and video are already compressed by their formats, so generic recompression rarely helps.

note: The bandwidth argument is sound: compressing in the client means fewer bytes on the network and in the cache, which is why client libraries such as pymemcache do it. 'Caches should never offer compression' is the teacher's opinion, reasoned out live, not an industry rule. Redis does compress internally where it is cheap and transparent (RDB files, optional list nodes).

Worst-case framing, which the teacher makes explicit later (L-0299). Databases cache hot table and index pages in RAM (for example the InnoDB buffer pool), so many database reads never touch disk.

The size threshold is wrong. Databases read from disk in fixed-size pages (8 kB in PostgreSQL, 16 KB by default in InnoDB), so reading 15 bytes and reading 1 KB cost the same single page IO. The large gap between RAM and disk (Jeff Dean's historical figures, c. 2009: about 100 ns per memory reference versus about 10 ms per disk seek; SSDs are much faster than spinning disks but still far slower than RAM) applies to both. The difference only narrows for large sequential reads (megabytes), where per-IO latency is spread over a lot of data.
precise_version: Disk reads happen in pages of 8-16 KB, so a 15-byte read and a 1 KB read cost the same disk IO; the gap between memory and disk narrows only for large sequential reads.

note: Right in spirit: InnoDB and PostgreSQL indexes are multi-level B-trees, and a lookup walks from root to leaf. Because each page holds hundreds of keys, the tree is shallow (a few levels even for very large tables, so log base ~hundreds of n, not log2 n). The upper levels are usually cached in the buffer pool, so a lookup often needs only one or two actual disk reads.

HTTP is indeed stateless (RFC 9110: each request 'can be understood in isolation'); cookies add sessions on top. On connections: HTTP/1.1 is persistent by default (RFC 9112 9.3). The Keep-Alive / 'Connection: keep-alive' header was the HTTP/1.0 opt-in, and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 forbid it. Statelessness (message semantics) and connection persistence are separate things.
precise_version: HTTP is stateless at the message level; connection reuse is separate: HTTP/1.0 opted in with Keep-Alive, HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent by default, and HTTP/2 connections are always persistent.

note: HTTP/2 connections are persistent (RFC 9113 9.1). WebSocket is a separate TCP-based protocol, but it starts as an HTTP request: its handshake is an HTTP Upgrade (RFC 6455 1.7), so it is set up over HTTP and then leaves it.

Closing after every response was the HTTP/1.0 default. HTTP/1.1, the version most web traffic still falls back to, uses persistent connections by default: the connection stays open unless either side sends 'Connection: close' or it times out (RFC 9112 9.3). In interviews, 'the server closes the connection after each response' is the HTTP/1.0 answer.
precise_version: In HTTP/1.0 the connection closed after each response unless Keep-Alive was negotiated; HTTP/1.1 keeps connections open by default until one side closes or a timeout hits.

note: Reasonable design advice; HTTP is defined as stateless (RFC 9110 3.3), and stateful long-lived channels are usually WebSockets or MQTT.

Teacher is right for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, which run over TCP (usually with TLS). HTTP/3, standardised in 2022 (RFC 9114), runs over QUIC, which is carried in UDP datagrams, so 'HTTP runs only on TCP' is no longer true either. The student's resource may have been describing HTTP/3.
precise_version: HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 run over TCP; HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which runs over UDP.

note: Right that HTTP semantics are not tied to TCP (RFC 9112: messaging is independent of the transport). But HTTP 'only presumes a reliable transport with in-order delivery', so it is not unrelated to the transport. Raw UDP gives neither guarantee. HTTP runs over UDP in practice only through QUIC (HTTP/3), which adds reliability on top of UDP.
precise_version: HTTP is independent of TCP but needs a reliable, ordered transport; HTTP/3 gets one over UDP via QUIC.
